title: Atlas AI POC scoping - latency/throughput SLOs
summary: POC scoping for Atlas AI to validate latency and throughput SLOs for user-facing completions. Discussed TTFT vs TPOT targets, baseline workload sizing (QPS, concurrency, token lengths), benchmark methodology (synthetic + production replay), model variants (7B quantized vs 13B fp16), caching/batching impact, and a 3-week POC timeline. Agreed next steps: Redwood to share benchmark plan and test data template, Atlas to provide sample traffic traces and success criteria spreadsheet.
topics: Workload sizing: QPS, concurrency, token length distributions
Benchmark plan: synthetic load, production replay, warm/cold starts
Targets: p95/p99 latency and tokens/sec SLOs
Measurement tooling and metrics to capture

Atlas to provide 72h production trace anonymized (by 2026-03-26)

transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2026-03-22 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Samira (Redwood SE), Diego (Redwood Solutions), Maya (Atlas Head of ML), Ethan (Atlas CTO), Liam (Atlas SRE), Sofia (Product)

Summary (auto-gen, might be imperfect): scoping call to align on latency/throughput SLOs, ttft vs tpot measurement, and POC plan.

[00:00] Jordan (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, then we'll jump into what you want out of the POC.
[00:08] Maya (Atlas): Hi all, Maya here. we're focused on the user chat product, 95% of requests are short completions 20-80 tokens, with about 10% long context summaries that can be 300-600 tokens. main ask is consistent sub-200ms perceived latency for interactive flows, and predictable cost.
[00:27] Samira (SE): great, couple clarifying q's: when you say perceived latency — are you measuring time to first token (TTFT) or time to full response (TPOT)? they differ a lot for longer outputs.
[00:36] Maya: good point — product cares a lot about TTFT for UI snappiness, we want p95 < 180ms ideally, p99 < 350ms for typical 1-2 sentence replies. for full answers (long ones) it's ok for TPOT to be higher, but we'd like tokens/sec to be predictable.
[00:52] Ethan (CTO): and reliability — we need SLOs we can commit to for launch. also security: SOC2 and SSO matter but we'll cover separately.
[01:02] Diego (Solutions): noted, we'll include security docs in the pack. on latency, we usually define two SLO dimensions: TTFT p95/p99 for interactive flows, and throughput/pipeline metrics — p95 token latency or tokens-per-second at target concurrency.
[01:15] Liam (SRE): quick context: our peak is 120 QPS for short completions, sustained, with spikes to ~220 qps during promotions. concurrency per instance is variable; we'd plan for 200 concurrent active users during peaks.
[01:29] Samira: OK that's helpful. to size the POC we want: 1) baseline model and infra test against your production trace, 2) a set of synthetic microbenchmarks for cold vs warm starts, batching, and KV cache hit/miss, and 3) comparison across model variants (7B quantized, 13B fp16).
[01:46] Maya: yes, and can you run both hosted and a dedicated config? we need to understand whether dedicated gives us better p99 tail behavior.
[01:54] Jordan: absolutely. our recommended POC is three weeks. Week 1: baseline runs + gather traces. Week 2: tuning (batching, quantization profiles, routing). Week 3: final benchmark and report.
[02:06] Sofia (Product): what's your typical TTFT numbers for a 7B quantized model on your hosted infra? ballpark.
[02:12] Samira: ballpark numbers, with batching disabled and small prompt sizes, TTFT p95 for 7B q8 models is ~80-120ms on A100-class instances in hosted. p99 tails can be ~220-350ms depending on cold starts and networking. For 13B fp16 it's more like p95 160-220ms, p99 400ms+. those are rough — depends on sequence length, kv cache hit rate, and batching.
[02:36] Ethan: those numbers align with our expectations. can you clarify how you measure TTFT vs TPOT exactly? we want reproducible methodology.
[02:44] Samira: yes. TTFT = time from request accept (ingress) to emission of first token byte. TPOT = time from token k to token k+1 averaged over the generation window (i.e., per-token latency). For end-to-end response time we also capture time to last token (TTLT) which is useful for long outputs.
[03:02] Diego: measurement plan steps: 1) replay 72h of anonymized traffic to capture distribution of prompt lengths and concurrency, 2) run microbenchmarks with controlled concurrency and arrival patterns (poisson, steady), 3) measure cold start scenarios (serverless or scale-up path) with controlled idle windows, 4) capture metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU util, memory, queue times, and per-request KV cache hit/miss.
[03:31] Liam: about KV cache — our prompts often repeat user prefixes, so cache hit rates could be high; measuring both cold miss and warm hit is important. is your harness able to simulate varying cache hit rates?
[03:41] Samira: yes we can instrument the harness to mark whether keys are pre-seeded and simulate x% warm hits. we'll run 0%, 50%, 90% hit scenarios.
[03:49] Jordan: on success criteria, how would you define pass/fail? e.g., p95 TTFT < 180ms AND p99 TTFT < 350ms for short completions and tokens/sec >= X for long responses.
[03:58] Maya: that seems reasonable. for tokens/sec we want stable 40-60 tokens/sec for long outputs at 4-6 concurrent gen streams. maybe call it p95 tokens/sec >= 45.
[04:10] Diego: we'll propose a matrix: rows are use-case buckets (short interactive, medium summaries, long synth), columns are metrics (TTFT p95/p99, TPOT p95, tokens/sec p95, cost $/1M tokens). each cell will have pass thresholds.
[04:25] Ethan: cost matters — we need to compare cost per 1M tokens between quantized 7B and 13B fp16, also remember infra overhead for dedicated clusters.
[04:34] Samira: we'll include unit economics. quick note on batching: batching increases throughput and lowers cost but can increase TTFT for single small requests if waiting for batch fill. we recommend always reporting both cold/no-batching and optimal-batching numbers along with SLO impact.
[04:50] Maya: yeah our app can't add 200ms of batching delay; we prefer small micro-batches or adaptive batching with timeouts <= 20ms.
[04:58] Samira: we can test adaptive batching configs (timeout 10ms, 20ms, 50ms) and report the observed TTFT p95/p99 tradeoffs and cost impact.
[05:07] Luis (note: mislabelled, could be Diego): question about measuring percents — do you include network egress time to user?
[05:12] Jordan: good callout — measurement baseline should include only service-side inference time; we'll also provide an end-to-end measurement that includes network latency from the target region to the client-facing endpoint. Atlas should decide which SLO they expose externally.
[05:23] Maya: we'll likely expose an end-to-end SLO but require Redwood to guarantee the inference portion.
[05:27] Samira: measurement tooling: we use a harness that can run both synthetic load (wrk/vegeta-style) and a replay harness that replays requests preserving inter-arrival times and token lengths. results are stored to a benchmark sheet and we'll attach raw traces and Grafana dashboards.
[05:40] Liam: instrumentation — we need histograms for p50/p95/p99, and raw request/response logs for debugging. also request ids must preserve cross-trace for correlation.
[05:49] Samira: agreed. we emit structured logs with request_id, model_variant, batch_size, kv_cache_hit, and timing fields. we can redact PII in replayed traces.
[05:58] Maya: any gotchas with cold starts for dedicated clusters vs hosted?
[06:02] Diego: dedicated usually has warmer tails because capacity is reserved, but you still need to consider model load time (if not preloaded) and autoscaler spin-up. for hosted we have prewarmed pools for common models to reduce cold-starts. we'll measure both.
[06:15] Ethan: timeline and deliverables again please.
[06:18] Jordan: three-week POC. deliverables: benchmark plan + harness config, initial baseline run report, tuning run results, final benchmark report with pass/fail matrix and cost comparison.
[06:29] Samira: week-level breakdown: Week 1: onboarding + baseline with your 72h trace; Week 2: tuning + model variant runs + adaptive batching testing; Week 3: sustained load and final report + executive summary.
[06:41] Maya: are you able to run a quick micro run today or tomorrow to sanity-check our sample?
[06:45] Samira: we can do a small sandbox run once you provide a small sample trace; that can validate harness and show early TTFT numbers.
[06:52] Jordan: ok next steps recap: Samira will share benchmark plan (tomorrow), Jordan will share POC engagement and pricing, Maya will send anonymized trace, and we'll schedule the sandbox run.
[07:02] Sofia: regarding security docs, you mentioned SOC2 and SSO — can you send the SOC2 report and SSO integration guide?
[07:08] Jordan: yes, will share SOC2 bridge and SAML integration docs; will also include KMS options for private deployments.
[07:16] Ethan: one more technical: when you report TPOT, is that per token on GPU or does it include scheduler queuing?
[07:22] Samira: it includes time inside the inference path and scheduler queuing inside the service boundary. we also report queue_time separately so you can see the breakdown.
[07:30] Maya: perfect. any blockers we foresee?
[07:33] Liam: main blocker is providing a clean anonymized traffic trace. we'll prioritize that.
[07:37] Jordan: great. thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with artifacts.

Auto Notes/Questions (sometimes imperfect):
- P95/P99 targets: agreed tentative targets for short completions: TTFT p95 <180ms, p99 <350ms. Long outputs: tokens/sec p95 >=45.
- POC timeline: 3 weeks, baseline + tuning + final.
- Measurement plan includes cold/warm starts, batching configs (10/20/50ms), kv cache hit scenarios (0/50/90%), and model variant comparison.

End of transcript.
